script: "She thought firefighters would save her fish—my warning almost killed them.". I was chilling in the kitchen when my cousin, let's call her Maya, storms in, eyes red from crying, clutching a broken 55‑gallon tank. "They're coming! They'll see it!" she screams, waving a shiny light‑up paw thing she bought on a dare. "Firefighters will spot the glow and pull the fish out before it's too late!" (I am already thinking, oh snap, this is a trainwreck). I slide on my sneakers, put my hands on her shoulders, and say, "Bruh, listen up. If it's a small fire, maybe they'll spot it, but if the flames hit the kitchen, they're not going to be holding a bucket of fish in a blaze. They're busy breathing life back into the house." I keep it short, because I know how quickly she dives into drama. "The best shot? Get the fire department to know there's a tank. Tell them the exact spot. Hope they don't smash it when they're dousing the flames." (I know, right?) She's yelling, "You're a horrible person! I hope you lose your dog in a fire for telling me this!" She's got the audacity to throw my past at me, but I've lived through two dog‑dies in a blaze, survived the smoke, and I am not about to let her think I am a saint. I am like, "Yeah, I lost my dogs, but I've learned how to keep a home safe. You're not asking me to be a hero, you're asking for realistic help." (Literally insane how she thinks I am the villain.) She's still fuming, her voice rising, "You're just a coward who's afraid of a little heat!" I pause, look at the cracked glass, the neon fish flopping uselessly. "Look, if the fire's intense, those little guys are dead in seconds. Firefighters don't have a spare crane for a 55‑gal tank. They're not going to pick up a heavy aquarium and move it. They're fighting a fire. They'll try to protect the house, not rescue your fish." (I know, right?) I drop the mic, I mean, drop my tone. "The only way you can save them is by making sure the fire department knows there's a tank. They'll at least try to keep the water intact. It's the only realistic chance." She glares, but I can see the doubt flicker. I don't need to keep blowing my own horn; I am already better than the drama. The fire alarm blares. I grab my phone, text the local 911 number, "Hey, we've got a 55‑gal aquarium in the living room, 2‑story house, please keep the water pool intact." I keep the line short, no fluff. "Just keep the fire out of the tank." She's still yelling, but I am already on the phone, my voice calm. (I am better than her, and I am not going to let her throw my past at me like a punch.) The fire trucks roll in. The squad leader says, "We've got a tank here, we'll do what we can." I watch as they set up hoses, aim at the walls, not the tank. The water starts to spill, the tank tilts, but the fish survive the first wave. They're trembling, but alive. (I am like, "See, I told you. You just need the right info.") The fire's out, the house is safe, the tank is intact. Maya walks over, eyes wet, looks at the fish, then at me. "I… I am sorry," she whispers. I nod, no drama, just a "I am here." I know I am not a hero, I am just realistic. And that's all I needed to do.
